19910:
English Bibles translate two Hebrew words, mishpat and tsedaqah, as 'justice' and 'righteousness'. They often appear as a pair, as in Amos's cry: 'let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream'.

Mishpat comes from the verb 'to judge' and covers court verdicts, fair rulings and the right order of things. Tsedaqah means being in the right, especially faithfully keeping one's commitments in a relationship. In the Psalms and prophets, God's tsedaqah is very often his saving action: he 'does justice' for the orphan and widow by rescuing them.

The New Testament word dikaiosyne carries both senses. It can mean God's own rightness, the right standing he gives to people, or the right living he produces in them. Paul's phrase 'the righteousness of God' is one of the most debated phrases in the Bible for exactly this reason.
19912:
Retributive comes from a Latin word meaning 'to pay back'. Retributive justice says that wrongdoing deserves a response that fits it. The punishment is not mainly about deterring others or reforming the offender, though it may do both; it is about honouring the truth that a real wrong has been done. A judge who lets the guilty walk free is not being kind but unjust.

Scripture often speaks this way. Abraham asks, 'Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?' God 'will by no means clear the guilty'. Paul says God 'will render to each one according to his works' and that 'the wages of sin is death'. The angel in Revelation praises God because his judgments are 'true and just'.

Classic defenders include Anselm, Calvin, Charles Hodge, Leon Morris and J. I. Packer. They see God's justice as part of his nature, not a policy he could change. Because God is holy, sin cannot simply be overlooked; it must be dealt with.
19913: Myth: 'An eye for an eye' was a licence for revenge. In context (Exodus 21, Leviticus 24, Deuteronomy 19) it was a rule for judges, setting a limit: the penalty must not exceed the harm. Jewish practice early on understood many such cases as monetary compensation. Jesus' teaching in Matthew 5:38-42 addresses personal retaliation, not the courts.
19915:
Restorative justice asks a different first question: not 'what does the offender deserve?' but 'who has been hurt, what do they need, and whose job is it to put things right?' The modern movement grew in the 1970s and 1980s, especially among Mennonites working in criminal justice. Howard Zehr's *Changing Lenses* (1990) is its classic text.

Christian defenders argue that this is close to the Bible's own heart. Biblical law required restitution: a thief repaid what he took plus a fifth, or more. Zacchaeus, on meeting Jesus, promised to repay fourfold. The prophets picture justice as the restoration of shalom, wholeness, for the whole community. Christopher Marshall argues that the New Testament's vision of justice is 'restorative' in this sense, and N. T. Wright reads 'the righteousness of God' in Paul as God's faithfulness to his covenant promise to put the world right.

Restorative views do not deny punishment. They argue that where punishment appears in Scripture, it serves a larger goal of repair rather than being an end in itself.
19916: Myth: 'Restorative justice means no consequences.' Its defenders insist on accountability: offenders must face the harm done and make amends. What they reject is punishment that does nothing to repair harm.
19918:
A third group argues that Scripture never forces a choice. Psalm 85 pictures 'righteousness and peace' kissing each other. Isaiah 11 describes the Messiah judging the poor with fairness and striking the wicked in the same breath.

Miroslav Volf, a Croatian theologian who lived through the Balkan wars, argued in *Exclusion and Embrace* (1996) that belief in God's final judgment is what frees victims to forgive: they do not have to take revenge because God will set things right. Tim Keller's *Generous Justice* (2010) stresses that the God who punishes oppression is the same God who defends the poor. Nicholas Wolterstorff grounds justice in the worth God gives to every person, which makes wrongs both deserve judgment and call for repair. Fleming Rutledge holds penal and victory language together in her study of the cross.

On this view, God judges evil because he loves what evil destroys. Judgment without restoration would be cold; restoration without judgment would pretend the wrong did not matter.
19919: What this means for the cross
19920:
If justice is chiefly retributive, the central question of the cross is: how can God forgive sinners and still be just? Paul's answer in Romans 3:26, that God is 'just and the justifier', is read as saying the penalty was really paid. This is the backbone of penal substitution.

If justice is chiefly restorative, the cross is God's decisive act of putting the world right: defeating evil, absorbing violence without returning it, forming a reconciled people, and opening the way to a healed creation. Christus Victor, recapitulation and healing models fit naturally here. Penal language is often reread as describing what sin does to us rather than what God inflicts.

Integrative readers argue that the cross does both. Sin is condemned in the flesh of Christ (Romans 8:3), and in the same act enemies are reconciled and powers disarmed (Colossians 1:20; 2:15).
19921: N. T. Wright accepts that Jesus bore the punishment of exile and death for Israel and the world, but places it within a covenant story of God putting the world right. Some Reformed critics, such as John Piper in *The Future of Justification* (2007), argue that his reading of 'righteousness' loses the imputation of Christ's righteousness to believers.
19922: What this means for the final judgment
19923:
All mainstream Christian traditions affirm a final judgment: Christ will judge the living and the dead. Scripture describes books opened, people judged by their works, and a separation between the righteous and the wicked.

Retributive readers see the final judgment as God publicly and finally giving each what is due. This usually goes with the traditional view of hell as conscious punishment, though some (conditionalists) argue that the just penalty is final destruction.

Restorative readers emphasise texts about God reconciling all things and making all things new. Some go further, to hopeful or confident universalism, in which even judgment aims at the eventual restoration of the judged. Most restorative writers stop short of that and say judgment is the removal of everything that destroys creation so that the new creation can flourish.

In both views the judgment is good news for victims: the evil done to them will not be ignored.
19924: What this means for church life
19925:
Jesus gives a process for dealing with sin in the church: go privately, then with witnesses, then to the church. The goal he names is 'you have gained your brother'. Paul tells the Corinthians to remove a man living in serious sin, but later urges them to forgive and comfort a repentant offender so he is not overwhelmed. Galatians 6:1 says to restore the one caught in sin 'in a spirit of gentleness'.

A strongly retributive instinct can lead churches to stress consequences, protection of the community and clear boundaries. A strongly restorative instinct can lead churches to stress reconciliation, listening to victims and the offender's return. Each has its danger: the first can become harsh and slow to welcome back; the second can push victims to forgive too quickly or leave offenders in positions where they can harm again.

The same debate shapes Christian thinking about prisons, the death penalty and national reconciliation. South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, was an explicit attempt to apply restorative principles after apartheid.
19926: Myth: 'Forgiveness means no consequences.' Most traditions distinguish forgiveness (giving up personal revenge and resentment) from trust and from legal consequences. Romans 12:19 forbids personal vengeance; Romans 13:4 still gives the state a role in punishing wrongdoing.
19928:
A frequent claim is that the Old Testament God is retributive and the New Testament God restorative. This idea goes back to Marcion in the second century, whom the church rejected. The Old Testament is full of mercy and restoration (Exodus 34:6, Hosea 11, Isaiah 40), and the New Testament contains some of the Bible's sternest warnings of judgment, many from Jesus himself.

Another is that retributive justice is the same as vengeance. Its defenders distinguish them: vengeance is personal, unmeasured and driven by anger; retribution is impartial, proportionate and carried out by rightful authority.

A third is that restorative justice is a secular or liberal import. Its modern form grew largely from Mennonite Christian practice, and its defenders argue its roots are in the biblical laws of restitution and the prophetic vision of shalom.

19967: Every Prophet and Apostle in the Bible
19968: Who were the prophets and apostles of the Bible, what did each one say or do, and what happened to them?
19969: A prophet in the Bible is someone who speaks for God, usually to warn, call people back to faithfulness, or announce what God is about to do. Sixteen prophets have books named after them, but dozens more appear in the stories, including several women, and the New Testament names prophets too. The Bible also names false prophets and gives tests for spotting them. An apostle is someone 'sent' with authority: above all the Twelve whom Jesus chose, plus Paul and a handful of others the New Testament also calls apostles. The Bible tells us how only a few of them died; most of what people 'know' about the deaths of the apostles comes from later tradition, which ranges from early and fairly reliable to late and legendary.
19970: 'Major' and 'minor' prophets refers to the length of their books, not their importance.
19971: Some of the most important prophets, such as Elijah, Elisha, Nathan and Samuel, wrote no book.
19972: The Bible names women prophets in both Testaments: Miriam, Deborah, Huldah, Isaiah's wife, Anna and Philip's four daughters.
19973: The four lists of the Twelve agree on the core but differ on one or two names, mainly Thaddaeus / Judas son of James.
19974: The New Testament also calls Paul, Barnabas, James the Lord's brother, Andronicus and Junia apostles, among others.
19975: The Bible records the deaths of only James son of Zebedee and Judas Iscariot among the Twelve; the deaths of Peter, Paul and James the Lord's brother are well attested outside the Bible; most other stories are later tradition.
19977:
The usual Hebrew word for prophet is navi, probably meaning 'one who is called' or 'one who calls out'. Older terms were ro'eh and hozeh, both meaning 'seer'; 1 Samuel notes that 'he who is now called a prophet was formerly called a seer'. Prophets were also called 'man of God'.

The clearest definition comes from God's words about Aaron: 'he shall be your mouth, and you shall be as God to him', and later 'Aaron your brother shall be your prophet'. A prophet is God's spokesperson. Deuteronomy says God will put his words in the prophet's mouth.

Predicting the future was only part of the job. Most prophetic speech is about the present: calling kings and people back to the covenant, condemning injustice and idolatry, and announcing judgment or hope as a result. Scholars sometimes put it as 'forth-telling' more than 'fore-telling'.

The full lists are in the in-app roster at /rosters?r=prophets.
19978: The major prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel
19979:
Isaiah prophesied in Jerusalem from about 740 to 700 BC, under kings Uzziah to Hezekiah. He warned Judah against trusting Assyria and Egypt instead of God, and announced a coming king and a suffering servant. Many scholars think chapters 40-66 come from later disciples speaking to exiles; traditional readers hold that Isaiah wrote the whole book.

Jeremiah prophesied from 627 BC until after Jerusalem fell in 586 BC. He told Judah that Babylon would win and that surrender was God's will, which got him beaten, imprisoned and thrown into a cistern. He also promised a new covenant written on the heart. The Bible last sees him taken to Egypt against his will.

Ezekiel was a priest taken to Babylon in 597 BC. From about 593 to 571 BC he spoke to the exiles in strange visions and acted-out signs: God's glory leaving the temple, a valley of dry bones coming to life, and a new temple.

Daniel served in the Babylonian and Persian courts from 605 to about 536 BC. His book combines court stories with visions of empires and a coming kingdom of God. Jewish Bibles place it among the Writings rather than the Prophets, and many scholars date the final book to about 165 BC; traditional readers hold to the sixth century.
19980: Myth: 'The minor prophets are less important.' The labels come from Augustine's time and refer only to length. The twelve shorter books were copied on a single scroll in Jewish tradition, called 'the Twelve'.
19982:
Hosea (about 755-715 BC) spoke to the northern kingdom, Israel. God told him to marry an unfaithful wife as a living picture of Israel's unfaithfulness and God's persistent love.

Amos (about 760 BC) was a shepherd and fig farmer from Tekoa in Judah sent north to Israel. He attacked luxury built on the backs of the poor. Jonah (about 780 BC) was the reluctant prophet sent to Nineveh; 2 Kings mentions him under Jeroboam II. Micah (about 735-700 BC) spoke to both Samaria and Jerusalem about injustice and named Bethlehem as the ruler's birthplace.

Nahum (between 663 and 612 BC) announced the fall of Nineveh. Zephaniah (about 630 BC, under Josiah) warned of the 'day of the LORD'. Habakkuk (about 605 BC) argued with God over why Babylon was allowed to triumph and learned that 'the righteous shall live by his faith'. Obadiah (after 586 BC) condemned Edom for joining in Jerusalem's fall.

After the exile, Haggai and Zechariah (520-518 BC) urged the returned exiles to rebuild the temple, and Malachi (about 450 BC) rebuked careless priests and promised the return of Elijah. Joel cannot be dated with confidence; suggestions range from the ninth to the fourth century BC. He described a locust plague and promised the Spirit poured out on all flesh.
19983: Dates for Joel, Obadiah and Malachi are educated guesses based on content. The book of Jonah is read by many scholars as a didactic story rather than a report; traditional readers take it as history, noting that Jesus refers to Jonah (Matthew 12:39-41).
19985:
Many of the Bible's prophets never wrote a book, or their writings are lost. The earliest are figures not usually thought of as prophets: Enoch (according to Jude), Abraham (whom God calls a prophet), Moses, the greatest prophet in the Old Testament's own estimate, and his brother Aaron.

In the days of the judges and early kings we meet Deborah, an unnamed prophet in Gideon's day, Samuel, Gad (David's seer), and Nathan, who rebuked David over Bathsheba. In the divided kingdom we meet Ahijah of Shiloh, Shemaiah, the man of God from Judah, Iddo the seer, Jehu son of Hanani and his father Hanani, Azariah son of Oded, Micaiah son of Imlah, Jahaziel, Eliezer son of Dodavahu, Zechariah son of Jehoiada (stoned in the temple court), Oded of Samaria, and the great pair Elijah and Elisha.

Chronicles also says that the temple musicians Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun 'prophesied' with lyres and cymbals, and it mentions prophetic records by Nathan, Gad, Iddo and others that have not survived. Late in the monarchy Uriah son of Shemaiah prophesied like Jeremiah and was executed by King Jehoiakim.
19987:
The Bible names women prophets in both Testaments. Miriam, Moses' sister, is called a prophetess and led Israel's song after the Red Sea crossing. Deborah was a prophetess and judge who summoned Barak to battle. Huldah was consulted by King Josiah's officials when the Book of the Law was found in the temple; her word confirmed coming judgment and set off Josiah's reform. Isaiah's wife is called 'the prophetess', though whether that means she prophesied or simply was the prophet's wife is debated.

In the New Testament, Anna, an elderly widow, is called a prophetess and spoke about the infant Jesus to all who were waiting for redemption. Philip the evangelist had four unmarried daughters who prophesied. Paul assumes that women pray and prophesy in church gatherings, and Peter's Pentecost sermon applies Joel's promise that 'your sons and your daughters shall prophesy'.

The Bible also names false prophetesses: Noadiah, who opposed Nehemiah; women who 'prophesy out of their own hearts' in Ezekiel; and the woman Jesus calls 'Jezebel' in Thyatira.
19988: Jewish tradition in the Talmud (Megillah 14a) counts seven prophetesses of Israel: Sarah, Miriam, Deborah, Hannah, Abigail, Huldah and Esther. Only Miriam, Deborah and Huldah are called prophetesses in the Hebrew Bible itself.
19990:
Luke's opening chapters are full of prophecy: Zechariah the priest prophesied at his son's birth, Simeon spoke over the baby Jesus in the temple, and Anna gave thanks. John the Baptist, Jesus said, was a prophet and 'more than a prophet', the messenger Malachi had promised.

Jesus himself was recognised as a prophet by the crowds and was called the prophet like Moses by Peter. He said a prophet is not without honour except in his home town.

In the early church, prophets were a recognised group. Prophets from Jerusalem came to Antioch, and one of them, Agabus, predicted a famine and later Paul's arrest. The church at Antioch had 'prophets and teachers': Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen and Saul. Judas Barsabbas and Silas were prophets who encouraged the church after the Jerusalem council. Paul lists prophets second after apostles and gives rules for testing prophecy in church. The author of Revelation calls his book 'the words of this prophecy'.
19991: Christians disagree on whether New Testament prophecy carried the same authority as Old Testament prophecy. Wayne Grudem argues it was a fallible report of what the Spirit brought to mind, to be weighed; Richard Gaffin and others argue it was revelatory and has ceased now that the canon is complete. See /debates/cessationism.
19992: False prophets and how to spot them
19993:
The Bible takes false prophecy seriously. Deuteronomy gives two tests: a prophet who leads people after other gods is false even if his sign comes true, and a prophet whose prediction fails has not spoken from the LORD. Jesus adds a third: 'you will recognise them by their fruits'. John adds a fourth: whether a spirit confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.

Named false prophets include Balaam (who blessed Israel under God's control but later led Israel into sin), the 450 prophets of Baal and 400 of Asherah on Mount Carmel, the old prophet of Bethel who lied to the man of God, Zedekiah son of Chenaanah who struck Micaiah, Hananiah son of Azur who broke Jeremiah's yoke, Pashhur, Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, Shemaiah the Nehelamite, Noadiah and Shemaiah son of Delaiah who tried to frighten Nehemiah, Bar-Jesus (Elymas) on Cyprus, 'Jezebel' at Thyatira, and the 'false prophet' of Revelation.

Some of these figures are complicated. Balaam really did receive words from God, and the old prophet of Bethel later spoke a true word of judgment. The Bible treats prophecy as something that must always be tested.
19994: The Twelve apostles and their names
19995:
Apostolos in Greek means 'someone sent'. Jesus chose twelve from his wider group of disciples, a number that echoes the twelve tribes of Israel. The New Testament lists them four times, and the lists vary in small ways, mostly because people had several names.

Simon was renamed Cephas (Aramaic) or Peter (Greek), both meaning 'rock'. James and John, sons of Zebedee, were nicknamed Boanerges, 'sons of thunder'. Thomas was also called Didymus, 'twin'. Matthew the tax collector appears as Levi son of Alphaeus in Mark and Luke's call stories, and most readers take them as the same man. Simon is called 'the Cananaean' (KJV 'Canaanite') in Matthew and Mark, from an Aramaic word for 'zealous', and 'the Zealot' in Luke and Acts.

The main puzzle is the tenth name. Matthew and Mark have Thaddaeus (some manuscripts of Matthew have Lebbaeus); Luke and Acts have Judas of James, usually translated 'son of James' (KJV 'brother of James'). John's Gospel mentions 'Judas, not Iscariot'. Most readers think these are one person with two names. John never gives a list and never names Bartholomew, but he features Nathanael, whom later tradition identified with Bartholomew.

After Judas Iscariot's death the eleven chose Matthias by lot to restore the number to twelve. See /rosters?r=apostles.
19996: Myth: 'The Bible says Bartholomew and Nathanael are the same person.' It does not. The identification is a later suggestion based on John pairing Nathanael with Philip, as the lists pair Bartholomew with Philip. It is plausible but unproven.
19998:
The New Testament uses 'apostle' in a narrow and a wider sense. In the narrow sense, an apostle had seen the risen Lord and been commissioned by him. Paul insists he meets that test, though 'as one untimely born'.

Besides the Twelve and Paul, the New Testament calls these people apostles: Barnabas (with Paul in Acts 14); James the Lord's brother (Galatians 1:19, depending on how the verse is read); Andronicus and Junia, who are 'of note among the apostles'; and, in 1 Thessalonians, probably Silas and Timothy as well as Paul. Epaphroditus is called the Philippians' 'messenger' (apostolos), and Paul speaks of 'messengers (apostoloi) of the churches', meaning sent delegates. Hebrews even calls Jesus 'the apostle and high priest of our confession'.

Paul also warns of 'false apostles' and 'super-apostles' at Corinth, and Revelation praises the Ephesians for testing those who called themselves apostles and were not.
